title.en: Arawidi the Fisher: the Alligator Ransoms Himself with a Wife
title.zh: 漁者阿拉威迪：鱷以女贖罪

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §142

summary.en: Arawidi, the medicine-man, dammed a favorite stream to retain water and fish for later visits; the otters destroyed it, so he appointed the woodpecker as watchman. Warned by a loud tapping of an alligator's proximity, he hurried along and clubbed the reptile so unmercifully that it offered him a girl for wife if he would only stop. Arawidi accepted these terms — but to this day the alligator shows the marks of the thrashing on its battered head, and in the notches along its tail.
summary.zh: 醫師阿拉威迪築壩蓄水魚；水獺毀之，遂以啄木鳥為守望。鳥叩木示警鱷至；彼疾至而痛擊之。鱷求止，許以女為妻。約成；然鱷首傷痕與尾上齒痕，至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Arawidi once, after fishing in a favorite stream, built a dam with the object of retaining both the water and the fish for use on subsequent visits. But the otters destroyed it, so he appointed the woodpecker to act as watchman. The latter warned him with a loud tapping of the proximity of an alligator: he hurried along and clubbed the reptile so unmercifully that it offered him a girl for wife if he would only stop. Arawidi accepted these terms, but to this day the alligator shows the marks of the thrashing on its battered head, and in the notches along its tail.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §142; not verbatim.

title.en: The War of the Birds: How They Got Their Distinctive Markings

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地（據布雷特）

texts.period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §143

summary.en: An Arawak hunter captured a Vulture, daughter of Anuamima the carrion crow; she laid aside her feathers, appeared before him as a beautiful girl, and became his wife, bearing him above the clouds and persuading her father and family to receive him. When he wished to visit his aged mother they set him on a high thorn-covered tree; spiders spun cords and birds eased his descent. For years he strove to regain his wife until the birds espoused his cause, assembled their forces, and bore him as their commander above the sky — where at last he was slain by a valiant young warrior resembling him in person and feature: it was his own son. The legend ends with the conflagration of the house of the Royal Vultures: the kiskedee who shirked the war was sentenced to wear his white cotton bandage continually; the trumpeter, quarreling over the spoil, arose with patches of gray; and the Owl, finding in the spoil a package that contained Darkness only, has never been able to endure the light of day.
summary.zh: 獵者得禿鷲婦——食腐鴉阿努阿瑪之女也；彼脫羽為人妻，攜夫上雲端。夫省母，遂被棄於棘樹之巔；蛛結繩、群鳥扶之而降。經年謀復，群鳥舉之為帥，上戰於天；末為相似之少戰士所殺——乃其親子也。鷲宮焚毀。臨陣託病纏白布之提提鳥，被罰永纏；爭利之鶴得灰斑；鴞得暗一包，故畏日光。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett 1880, summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: An Arawak hunter captures a Vulture, daughter of Anuamima. She lays aside her feathers, appears before him as a beautiful girl, becomes his wife, bears him above the clouds, and after much trouble persuades her father and family to receive him. All then goes well until he expresses a wish to visit his aged mother, when they discard him and set him on the top of a very high tree, the trunk of which is covered with formidable prickles. He appeals to all the living creatures around: then spiders spin cords to help him and fluttering birds ease his descent, so that at last he reaches the ground in safety.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143 (from Brett); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then follow his efforts, extending over several years, to regain his wife. At length the birds espouse his cause, assemble their forces, and bear him as their commander above the sky. At last he is slain by a valiant young warrior resembling him in person and feature: it is his own son. The legend ends with the conflagration of the house of the Royal Vultures.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143 (from Brett); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Kiskedee, though a valiant little bird, disliked the war, and bandaged his head with white cotton, pretending to be sick; but being detected, was sentenced to wear it continually. He is noted for his hostility to hawks and other large birds. The Warracaba, the trumpeter bird, and the kingfisher quarreled over the spoil and knocked each other over in the ashes: the former arose with patches of gray, while the other became gray all over. The Owl discovered among the spoil a package done up with care, which he found to contain Darkness only; he has never been able since to endure the light of day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143 (from Brett); not verbatim.

title.en: The Deer and the Turtle Exchange Footwear

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §143A

summary.en: The Deer met the Turtle one day while cleaning his hoofs — for in those days turtle wore hoofs and the deer had claws — and said: 'My friend, you have nice sandals. Let me have a trial of them.' The Turtle, very proud of them, handed them over, receiving in exchange the Deer's nails. When the Deer put on the hoofs he found he could walk ever so much quicker, and trotted off. The poor Turtle found his progress impeded, and stood still waiting every minute for the Deer to return — but he never did so.
summary.zh: 一日鹿遇龜理蹄——古時龜有蹄而鹿有利爪——曰：『友哉，汝履甚美，借吾一試。』龜愛其履而與之，易以鹿爪。鹿得蹄而行愈疾，遂逸去。龜步艱難，立而待其還——竟不返。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Deer met the Turtle one day, while cleaning his hoofs — for in those days turtle wore hoofs and the deer had claws — and said: 'My friend, you have nice sandals. Let me have a trial of them.' The Turtle, who was very proud of them, said: 'Certainly. Why not?' and handed them over, receiving in exchange the Deer's nails. When the Deer now put on the hoofs, he found that he could walk ever so much quicker than before, and trotted off. The poor Turtle, however, found his progress impeded, and stood still, waiting every minute for the Deer to return — but he never did so.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §143A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Unlucky Hunter and Black Tiger Tobe-horoanna

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §144

summary.en: A man unlucky in hunting had two brothers-in-law who always brought home game; 'As he has no luck, we will lose him away.' They sent him on a route leading to the lair of Tobe-horoanna — an immense, cruelly savage beast, a tiger only when walking in the bush, at home 'like a man, people'. Chased round an immense tree, the man just managed to reach the animal's hindquarters and cut off both its heels; then he shot it through the neck and finished it with a knife. His brothers-in-law could hardly believe him until he boldly trampled on the carcass; the old father gave him another daughter, the brothers built him a bigger house, and he was henceforth recognized as chief of the settlement.
summary.zh: 一獵者屢空；二內兄常滿載，曰：『彼無運，吾儕當棄之。』乃導之行黑皮虎多貝霍羅安納之徑——巨獸也，行林則為虎，居家則如人。人繞巨樹而奔，伺其後而斷其雙踵；復射其頸，以刀了之。眾不信；彼直踐其屍。岳父以次女妻之，內兄為築大屋，遂為村長。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was once a man who had two brothers-in-law. While he was one of the unluckiest of mortals, they invariably returned home of an afternoon with plenty of game. They said: 'As he has no luck, we will lose him away.' So one day they took him into the bush, all three going in together, but soon told him to go in one direction while they went in another. The route the two wicked brothers instructed him to follow led to the lair of Tobe-horoanna — signifying in Warrau 'Tiger-black-skin', the name given to an immense, cruelly-savage beast believed to exist in the depths of the forest, a tiger only when it goes for a walk in the bush, at home 'like a man, people'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §144; not verbatim.

passages.text: He went on and on until, hearing a great rushing noise approaching, he saw the Tobe-horoanna coming and ran as fast as he could toward an immense tree, Black Tiger after him. Running round and round the trunk, the one after the other, the man just managed to reach the animal's hindquarters and cut off both its heels; Tiger sat down, for it could not walk at all now. Next the man shot it through the neck with his arrow, and after finishing the job with a knife went back home. His brothers-in-law never doubted they had seen the last of him — and were greatly surprised at his arrival, making excuses for their absence.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §144; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he told them he had actually killed the Tobe-horoanna, the two brothers-in-law as well as their old father could hardly believe him, but insisted on being taken to the place. At a distance they saw Black Tiger on the ground; all except the man who had killed it were afraid to go near. To show them that he spoke true he boldly went up and trampled on the carcass — only then would the old man approach. On arrival home the old father-in-law gave him another daughter, so that he had two wives now; the brothers-in-law built him a bigger house, and he was henceforth recognized as Aijamo — chief, head-man of the settlement.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §144; not verbatim.

title.en: Adaba the Tree-Frog Teacher of Hunters

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §145

summary.en: Three brothers hunting far from home left their sister at the benab and brought back only a powis day after day. An Adaba tree-frog singing Wang! Wang! in a hollow tree nearby heard her complaint — 'Stop that noise and bring me some game to eat' — changed himself into a man, and returned with meat. He laughed at the fungus growing all over their arrows — 'So long as you do not remove this stuff your arrows will never shoot straight' — cleaned them, tied a fishing-line between two trees for target practice, and taught them his own trick of pointing the arrow into the sky so that in its descent it stuck into the creature's back. The brothers took him home as brother-in-law; but when his wife splashed him at the pond he turned back into a frog and hopped into the hollow tree, where he still is — and their luck went with him.
summary.zh: 三兄弟獵於遠處，留妹於棚，日惟得一鷸。棚側空心樹中樹蛙阿達巴聞其歎，化人出，攜肉而歸；見其箭遍生菌而笑：『不去此物，箭必不直。』為拭箭、懸釣線為的、教仰天射而落其背之秘。兄弟攜之歸為妹夫。後妻浴水潑之，蛙復本形而入空心樹，至今在焉；其運亦隨之去。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There were once three brothers who went out to hunt, taking their sister with them. Far out in the bush they built a banab, where the sister was left all alone while they wandered about in search of game; every day the three brothers went hunting in all directions, but never brought back any meat except a powis. Now there was an Adaba [tree-frog] living in a hollow tree containing a little water close to the banab, and one afternoon he was singing his song 'Wang! Wang! Wang!' when the girl heard him. 'What are you holloing for?' she said; 'it would be much better if you stopped that noise and brought me some game to eat.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §145; not verbatim.

passages.text: So the Adaba stopped holloing, changed himself into a man, went away into the bush, and returned in about two hours with some meat for her. 'Cook this before your brothers come back: as usual they will return with nothing.' Adaba spoke truly. The brothers' surprise may be imagined when they saw their sister barbecuing plenty of meat and a strange man lying in one of their hammocks — a strange man indeed, with stripes all the way down his thin legs. He burst into a hearty laugh at the fungus growing everywhere on their arrows, saying that so long as they did not remove this stuff their arrows would never shoot straight; he cleaned them, tied a fishing-line between two trees, and had each brother's arrow stick into the very center of it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §145; not verbatim.

passages.text: Adaba had a curious trick in shooting with his arrow: instead of taking aim at an animal direct, he would point the arrow up into the sky, so that in its descent it would stick into the creature's back. The brothers became such adepts that they never missed anything, took him home, and made him their brother-in-law. But one day his wife splashed water over him at the pond, and directly she put her hands on him he turned himself into a frog again and hopped away into the hollow tree, where he still is. The three brothers often went out hunting after that, but they never brought back anything like the quantity of game they used to get when Adaba was present.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §145; not verbatim.

title.en: Why Black Tiger Killed the Indians

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §148

summary.en: Tobe-horoanna caught a young man in the bush, put him in the pot, and said: 'You must not be frightened. I do not intend killing, cooking, and eating you.' His captors fed him a whole bush-hog and a calabashful of cassiri, forcing him to drink until he vomited; his sister defended him, and when he returned from the bush with ten dried bush-hogs he won the tiger woman as wife. She bore him twin sons who growled like thunder — 'but the same row which the Black Tiger nation always made when they traveled in the bush'. Homesick, he visited his mother, who in drunken fury upbraided him for bringing home a tigress and slew him and his wife; the twin boys escaped, and their uncle Tobe-horoanna, hearing all, changed into a Black Tiger again, trotted off to the drinking-party, and killed everyone — mother, daughter, and all the guests.
summary.zh: 黑皮虎獲一青年，置之釜而曰：『毋懼，吾不烹汝。』令食全豚、盡飲一葫蘆之酒，嘔則再灌。其妹護之，許以女妻。婦生雙子，吼聲如雷——黑皮虎族行林之常聲也。夫省母；母醉怒，罵其娶虎婦，殺之並殺其妻。雙子遁歸；舅聞之，復化黑皮虎，奔至宴所，盡殺母、女與賓客。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: One day Tobe-horoanna caught a young man out in the bush and, dragging him home, put him inside the pot, saying: 'You must not be frightened. I do not intend killing, cooking, and eating you. You are going to live.' His brother and sister came home: 'Have you fed him? Well, give him a bush-hog, and if he does not finish the whole of it, we shall have to finish him.' The man did his best to eat, but by the time he had stowed away the two hind legs his belly could hold no more; they handed him a calabashful of cassiri, and when he vomited it, Black Tiger had his brother hold him while he should pour more down — until their sister told them to let the man alone, as she had taken a liking to him and wanted to live with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §148; not verbatim.

passages.text: They told him to go into the bush and hunt, so as to show them that he could support a wife; when he returned with ten dried bush-hogs, Tobe-horoanna said: 'All right! I am satisfied. You can have my sister.' Thus the man came to live a long time there with his Tiger wife, who ultimately bore him twin sons. As the children grew they growled and made a noise just like Naharani [thunder]; their mother told him it was nothing, 'but the same row which the Black Tiger nation always made when they traveled in the bush.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §148; not verbatim.

passages.text: Homesick, he visited his mother, who upbraided him for bringing home such a daughter-in-law — could he not see she was not 'a proper people' but a tigress, who would fall upon and destroy him some day? In her drunken fury she and her daughter killed him: his wife did her best to defend him, but they slew her also. His two boys managed to make good their escape and reached home in safety. Uncle Tobe-horoanna asked them where their father and mother were; hearing what had happened, he became very angry, changed himself into a Black Tiger again, trotted off to the place where they were all drinking, and killed everyone — mother, daughter, and all the guests.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §148; not verbatim.

title.en: Bravery Rewarded with a Wife: Sika-waka the Jigger-plenty
title.zh: 勇者得妻：多蚤之錫卡瓦卡

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §147

summary.en: Some men out hunting found a dead mora tree overgrown with daiha creeper and went with their wives to strip the bark for apron-belts — a little boy along for company, climbing a manicole tree. The noise of their wooden staves drowned the roar of an immense Tiger, which appeared among them and killed every one except the boy, who slid down, jumped into the corial, and shoved off as Tiger, gorged with human flesh, came after him too late. Next morning he told the men; they found the mutilated bodies, and all but two turned cowards and climbed for safety — Tobe-akuba and Sika-waka, the latter half-lame with the jiggers in his feet, fought the tiger alone and destroyed it. Tobe-akuba taunted the tree-climbers, gave Sika-waka his daughter to wife, and the dogs needed twenty days to devour what a big brute he must have been.
summary.zh: 獵者與妻往取岱哈藤皮；小兒登棕上望。虎至而盡殺之；小兒滑下，解舟而遁。翌日告眾；眾尋屍，見妻胸被齧。群皆怯而登樹；惟多貝阿庫巴與足患沙蚤之錫卡瓦卡二人戰而斃虎。庫巴嘲之曰：『爾足無蚤而怯，彼殘而敢。』乃以女妻之。犬二十日方食盡虎肉——其巨可知。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Some men were out hunting, when they came across a dead mora tree that had a daiha creeper growing over it. So soon as they reached home they told their wives, who arranged to go next day to gather the bark for apron-belts. They took a little boy with them for company, and, having reached the spot, started removing the bark while the child amused himself by climbing into a manicole tree. The noise made by their wooden staves drowned the roar of an immense Tiger, which suddenly appeared among them and, without giving them a chance of escape, killed every one — all except the little boy, who could see everything that took place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §147; not verbatim.

passages.text: He saw the Tiger eat a piece out of this body and a bit out of that, finally dragging the bodies into the bush. As soon as the coast was clear the child slid down the tree, ran to the landing, jumped into the corial and shoved off — only just in time, because Tiger was after him, but unable to catch up with him on account of being gorged with human flesh. Next morning he told the men everything, and how all their women had been killed. Going to the spot they saw only blood, and one after another the mutilated bodies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §147; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last they came across the Tiger, but what with the ghastly scenes they had just witnessed, all except two of the search party turned cowards, and climbed for safety up the neighboring trees. The two exceptions were Tobe-akuba and Sika-waka [Jigger-plenty], the latter half-lame owing to the jiggers that infested his feet. These two men alone fought that tiger and ultimately destroyed it. Tobe-akuba then taunted the others: 'You have no jiggers in your feet as this man has, and yet none of you dared come help me as he did.' After leaving all their dogs to eat Tiger's carcass, they returned home, where Tobe-akuba picked out the jiggers from Sika-waka's feet and gave him his daughter to wife. It took the dogs twenty days to consume all the flesh — you can easily learn from this what a big brute he must have been.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §147; not verbatim.

title.en: Bamu and the Frog: How Mankind Was Divided

region.zh: 圭亞那（據布雷特）

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §149

summary.en: To account for the division of mankind into races, Brett gives the little story of Bamu. He came to visit some friends who were about to go frog-hunting — hunting, none of your small-sized frogs, but frogs as large as bush-hogs. Bamu, a braggart, refused a cudgel: he would jump on the back of the first frog he met and twist its neck around. The Chief of the Frogs heard him boast and squatted close to the river in front of his path; Bamu jumped — and so did the Frog, right into the water, carrying him to the opposite bank, where it jerked him off. Too ashamed to swim back and be laughed at again, Bamu remained on that side, begat children, and became separated from us.
summary.zh: 布雷特以此小故事釋人種之分。巴穆赴友人蛙獵——所獵非小蛙，乃大如野豬之蛙也。彼自誇無須兵器，將躍上蛙背而扭其頸。蛙之王聞而蹲於河畔道上；巴穆一躍，蛙亦躍，竟負之渡河，至彼岸而拋之。巴穆羞不敢泅回受哂，遂留彼岸，生兒育女，與吾儕分為兩族。

sensitivity.note: Guiana tradition from Brett 1880, retold in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Bamu came to visit some friends who were about to go frog-hunting — hunting for none of your small-sized frogs but for frogs as large as bush-hogs. They told Bamu to take a cudgel and come with them, but he, being a braggart, said that he did not want any weapons, but would jump on the back of the first frog he met and twist its neck around.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §149 (from Brett); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Chief of the Frogs heard him boast, and purposely squatted close to the river just in front of the path along which Bamu was coming. Bamu made a jump and so did the Frog, right into the water, the latter taking him over to the opposite bank, where he jerked him off. When his friends first saw Bamu on the Frog's back they started laughing, and chaffed him to twist the Frog's neck and bring the dead animal over. But he was too much ashamed to swim back and be laughed at again. So it came to pass that Bamu remained on that side, begat children, and became separated from us.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §149 (from Brett); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Man Fooled the Tiger

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §150

summary.en: An Indian stayed drinking paiwarri at a distant settlement till midnight, refused the house-master's warning that an immense Tiger prowled the road — 'I am not afraid, and if I meet him I will kill him' — staggered off, and fell dead asleep at the very spot where the Tiger used to cross. Tiger found him, sniffed him, sat down on him, then cleared a pathway of bushes to drag the body home. Carried slung across the brute's back, the man caught the bushes with his teeth and hands to impede progress; the Tiger cleared more bushes, the man fooled his captor three or four times, and when slung once more struck the animal's head just above the ear with his stone-tipped club and killed him.
summary.zh: 一印第安人宴飲至半夜，不聽主人之誡——『吾何懼，遇虎則殺之』——蹣跚而歸，倒臥於虎慣經之道。虎嗅之，坐其身，拔叢開道以曳之歸。人被負於背，以齒手攀叢阻行；虎再拔叢；如是者三四。虎復負之，人乃以石首杖擊其耳上，斃之。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: An Indian went to a somewhat distant settlement to drink paiwarri, and by midnight, the drinks being finished, started on the return journey, although the house-master warned him not to leave then but to wait for daybreak, because an immense Tiger was known to be prowling about. 'Oh! never mind. I am not afraid, and if I meet him I will kill him.' So saying, he hung his poto (stone-club) over his arm and went out into the darkness, staggered along more or less drunk, and fell dead asleep on the road just about the very spot where the Tiger of which he had been warned used to cross.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §150; not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger found him lying there motionless in the early morning, felt and sniffed him all over, and finally sat down on him. This sobered the Indian. Tiger, seeing that he was alive, started pulling down the bushes so as to clear a pathway along which he could drag the body to his lair. Having cleared a few yards, the animal returned and slung the man over his back, head and arms hanging over one flank and legs over the other.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §150; not verbatim.

passages.text: This gave the man his opportunity: as the animal carried him along he caught hold of the bushes with his teeth and hands and so impeded Tiger's progress. Thinking the pathway still too narrow, the Tiger replaced the burden on the ground and pulled down more bushes. The Indian thus fooled his captor some three or four times and, having collected his wits, watched for the tiger to sling him once more on his back — no sooner had Tiger done so than he struck the animal's head just above the ear with his stone-tipped club, and thus killed him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §150; not verbatim.

title.en: The Search for the Stone Ax

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §151

summary.en: Among the Arawaks tradition has it that the old stone axes — walikinor-haro, 'the ancients' axe' — came from a far distant country, so far away that it took years for those who went in search of them to get back home again. A corial full of people with a very old medicine-man in charge set out, carrying cassava-sticks to plant at the spot where the axes were found, so they might reap food for the home journey — it might be years before they would see their wives and children again. Down the river they paddled, out into a sea of blue water with so many submerged rocks that there was great risk of the vessel being smashed. The old man told the crew to shoot arrows into this blue water: where an arrow sank, there danger lurked; where one floated, there the corial was enabled to pass. Thus the sea was crossed in safety — and through all the extraordinary adventures of the journey runs an ethical undercurrent: disobedience to one's elders never remains unpunished.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦克人言古石斧（『先人之斧』也）來自絕遠之地，覓者經年乃返。一舟人皆行，老醫師領之；載薯種以植於斧所，俾收成為歸糧——經年始見妻兒也。泛入藍海，暗礁林立，舟將碎；老者令射箭入水：沈者險，浮者可過。遂安渡——而全篇之旅，皆寓長者之命不可違，違必受罰。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Among the Arawaks tradition has it that the old stone axes — walikinor-haro, literally 'the ancients' axe' — came from a far distant country, from a place so far away that it took years for those who went in search of them to get back home again. Many a bizarre exploit is told in connection with the search for these stone implements, and through most of these extraordinary adventures flows a sort of ethical undercurrent conveying the lesson that disobedience to one's elders never remains unpunished.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §151; not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a corial full of people, with a very old man, a medicine-man, in charge. They were about to search for some stone axes, but as they had a long, long way to go, their wives whom they were leaving at home had made a plentiful supply of cassava; in the boat they took also cassava-sticks, so that when they reached the spot where the axes were found they might plant them, and after reaping obtain cassava for their home journey. It might be years before they would see their wives and children again. Down the river they paddled, out into a sea which had blue water in it, and with so many submerged rocks that there was a great risk of the vessel being smashed to pieces. The old man told the crew to shoot arrows into this blue water: where an arrow sank, there did danger lurk; where one floated, there the corial was enabled to pass. The sea was ultimately crossed in safety by this means.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §151; not verbatim.

title.en: The Huri Fish Nation

region.en: Across the blue water (Arawak otherworld journey)
region.zh: 藍海之外（阿拉瓦克異境）

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §152

summary.en: The old man told them they were approaching the Huri Fish Nation, and that when they reached the landing place they would see large numbers of fish lying in the sand — but they were neither to shoot them with their arrows nor chop them with their knives, because they were really men and women. One of the crew stealthily arose in the night, shot one of the fish, roasted and ate it alone. At dawn a large body of Indians came and demanded the head of the crew: one of their men was lost. Each visitor was given a calabashful of boiling water to drink so as to vomit; the offender, called last and compelled, vomited all the bits of the forbidden fish — 'You are the one that killed our brother' — and was thrown into the boiling pot in the presence of all his comrades.
summary.zh: 老者言將至呼里魚族：灘上魚滿，然皆男女也，毋射毋斫。夜一人潛起，射魚炙而私食之。黎明土人大至，索舟長，言族人失其一。以沸水飲客，令各嘔吐；犯者最後被召，強飲而嘔出所食之魚——『汝殺吾兄弟者也』——當眾投之沸釜。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The old man told them that they were approaching the Huri Fish Nation, and that when they reached the landing place they would see large numbers of fish lying in the sand, but they were neither to shoot them with their arrows nor chop them with their knives, because they were really men and women. What the old man said actually happened when they landed that night. But when all the others slept, one of the crew stealthily arose, went down to the water-side, drew his bow, shot one of the fish, roasted it without making any noise, ate it all by himself, and returned to his hammock.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §152; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning at early dawn a large body of Indians came trooping down to the encampment, and asked for the head of the boat's crew: 'One of our men is lost; we suppose some of your party have killed him.' Arrived at their own camp, they put water into a large pot over the fire, and when boiled gave to each of the visitors, beginning with the old man, a calabashful of the hot water to drink, so as to make each one vomit. The individual who had killed and roasted the fish was called last: as soon as he had drunk, he vomited all the bits of the forbidden fish. 'You are the one that killed our brother.' Whereupon they threw him into the boiling pot in the presence of all his comrades. The old man and his crew were now free to resume their journey.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §152; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Ant-eater Fooled the Man

region.zh: 阿拉瓦克異境之旅

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §153

summary.en: Reaching another country, the party woke up one morning very hungry, and the old man sent all his crew out a-hunting: no matter what animal they saw, they were to shoot or club it. One disobedient man slept away most of the day and went out only as the sun was in the west, taking only his knife. Not far along he came on a large ant-eater lying fast asleep in the shade, touched it with his big toe — 'I wonder what has killed you; but as you are yet quite fresh, I will take you home' — and went off slowly to find a bark-strip to tie it up. When he got back, the ant-eater was gone. 'You are a fool. The ant-eater was not dead, but only sleeping. Didn't you see it blowing?' They all laughed heartily at him, and he recognized only too late that if he had obeyed orders he would have had something good to eat.
summary.zh: 至他國，晨起皆饑；老者令全隊出獵，見獸即射或擊之。一人違命，酣睡半日，日西乃出，僅攜刀。不遠遇大食蟻獸睡於蔭；以足趾觸之曰：『何物殺汝？尚鮮，吾當負歸。』徐尋樹皮束之；及返，獸已杳。老者曰：『愚哉！彼非死乃睡也，不見其鼻息乎？』眾大笑；彼悔之晚矣——聽命則有美餐矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Reaching another country, the party woke up one morning very hungry. The old man sent all his crew out a-hunting, and told them that no matter what animal they saw, they were to shoot with their arrows or club it, as the circumstances warranted. With one exception, they all did as they were told and brought back late in the afternoon plenty of game. The disobedient one was tired, went to sleep in his hammock the greater part of the day, and went out into the bush only as the sun was already in the west, taking only his knife with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §153; not verbatim.

passages.text: He had not walked very far when he came on a large ant-eater lying fast asleep in the shade. So soundly was it sleeping that it allowed the man to come quite close; then he touched it with his big toe and said: 'Hullo! I wonder what has killed you; but as you are yet quite fresh, I will take you home.' He went in search of a piece of strong bark-strip wherewith to tie up the animal, sauntering about carelessly; but when he did get back to the spot, the ant-eater was gone! He looked up, and down, and all about: 'This is the very spot where I saw it lying dead. Some one must have taken it away.' The old man said: 'You are a fool. The ant-eater was not dead, but only sleeping. Didn't you see it blowing?' They all laughed heartily at him, and he recognized only too late that if he had obeyed orders he would have had something good to eat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §153; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Indians Learned to Paddle

region.zh: 阿拉瓦克異境之旅

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §154

summary.en: Another country they visited was peculiar in that its inhabitants could travel in their corials only with the tide: they had paddles but held them edgeways instead of broadside to the water, and when the tide turned they drove a long pole into the stream bed and made fast until it turned again. The old medicine-man leader changed himself into a bunia bird and yelled out its note, Tarbaran! Tarbaran! The paddlers were annoyed — 'Nonsense! If we were to take the broadsides of our paddles and hit you on the head with them, how would you like it?' — but the bird still shrieked, until each paddler at last turned his paddle broadside to the water and found he could travel three times as fast as before. They never used their paddles edgewise again — and there is an island in the Essequibo just above Groote Creek called Woman's Pole, where women paddling edgewise once drove their pole so firmly into the mud that it could not be got out again: the timbers, grasses, and sand collected round it, forming the present island.
summary.zh: 至一國，其民惟隨潮而行：有槳而側之於水，潮逆則插長竿繫舟以待。老醫師化為斑鳩，鳴曰：塔巴然！塔巴然！槳者怒曰：『謬哉！以槳面擊爾首，爾意如何？』鳥終不已；眾乃轉槳以面迎水，行速三倍。自此不復側槳。埃斯塞基博河顧特溪上有一島，名『婦人之竿』——昔婦人側槳行，竿插泥太牢而不得出；木草沙積其周，遂成今島。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Another country which they visited in the course of their peregrinations was peculiar in that its inhabitants could travel in their corials only with the tide: they had paddles, but did not know how to use them in the proper way, holding the paddle edgeways instead of broadside to the water. When the tide turned against them they would drive a very long pole into the bottom of the stream, and make fast their corial to it until the tide turned again. The old leader, who was a medicine-man, changed himself into a bunia, and yelled out its note, 'Tarbaran! Tarbaran!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §154; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of the people paddling in this curious fashion were annoyed, and remarked: 'Nonsense! If we were to take the broadsides of our paddles and hit you on the head with them, how would you like it?' But the bird still continued shrieking 'Tarbaran! Tarbaran!' and would not stop. So each paddler at last turned his paddle round and pulled it broadside with the water, and found he could travel three times as fast as before; they never used their paddles edgewise again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §154; not verbatim.

passages.text: There is an island in the Essequibo just above Groote Creek called 'Woman's Pole'. The story goes that once upon a time the women there were traveling in the old-fashioned way with the paddles edgewise; when the tide turned against them they fixed the pole as usual in the mud, but drove it in so firmly that they could not get it out again. The timbers, grasses, and sand collected round it, forming the present island.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §154 (footnote); not verbatim.

title.en: The Big Bats of the Bat Tribe

region.zh: 阿拉瓦克異境之旅

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §155

summary.en: At nightfall the search party reached a landing in the country of the Bat Tribe, and the old man warned his crew that it was very dangerous to sling their hammocks on the trees, because the Bats here were as large as cranes: he called on them to build an enclosed camp. One slothful young man refused to come inside, fixing his hammock between two trees — he did not believe that the Bats, however big, would hurt him before morning. Late in the night, in the pitch dark, they heard him entreating to be allowed in; but they said: 'No. We cannot open the door now. You must bear what comes on you.' When they opened the door in the morning, all that was left of him was some bones: the Bats had sucked him dry indeed.
summary.zh: 夜抵蝙蝠族之國；老者誡曰：樹間懸床甚危，此間巨蝠大如鶴；令築圍棚。一懶兒不信，縛床兩樹之間而宿於外。夜半黑甚，聞其哀求入內；眾曰：『不可啟門，汝自承其果。』晨啟門視之，惟餘骸骨——巨蝠吮之殆盡矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The search party continued their journey, and at nightfall reached a landing. Now this was in the country of the Bat Tribe, and the old man warned his crew that it was very dangerous for them to sling their hammocks on the trees, because the Bats here were as large as cranes. He therefore called on them to build an inclosed camp — a banab with covered sides. One young man, however, was slothful and very backward in assisting the others to build the shelter: he did not believe that the Bats, however big they were, would hurt him before the morning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §155; not verbatim.

passages.text: In spite of the old man's entreaties, he refused to come into the inclosure, but, fixing his hammock between two trees, rested outside; the others slung their hammocks inside the banab. Late in the night, when it was quite dark, they heard the man outside entreating to be allowed to come in. But they said: 'No. We cannot open the door now. You must bear what comes on you.' And when they opened the door in the morning, all that was left of the individual was some bones. The Bats had sucked him dry indeed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §155; not verbatim.

title.en: The Magic Boat

region.zh: 阿拉瓦克異境之旅

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §156

summary.en: On and on the party went, and in the afternoon came to a landing where there was a beautiful canoe with a paddle inside it. But the old man warned them to leave it strictly alone: 'Don't any of you get into that boat, because if you do, even without touching the paddle, you will be carried off immediately, and we shall never see you again.' They all took heed except one man, and went to sleep. He could not sleep: the more he thought of the boat, the greater was his desire to look at it again. He slipped out of his hammock, gazing at its graceful lines, admiring it more and more, until he finally jumped in. No sooner had he done so than the vessel went off with him, and neither boat nor occupant was seen again.
summary.zh: 行行復行行；午後抵一停處，有美舟在焉，槳在其內。老者誡曰：『毋登此舟！雖不觸其槳，亦必立被載去，永不復見。』眾皆聽命而睡；惟一人不能寐，思舟愈甚，遂潛出，漸近而賞其美，終一躍而入。甫登，舟即載之而去，人與舟皆不復見。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: On and on the party went, and in the afternoon they came to a landing where there was a beautiful canoe with a paddle inside it. But the old man warned them to leave it strictly alone. 'Don't any of you get into that boat, because if you do, even without touching the paddle, you will be carried off immediately, and we shall never see you again.' They all took heed, except one man, and went to sleep.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §156; not verbatim.

passages.text: This one man kept awake and could not sleep: the more he thought of the boat, the greater was his desire to go and have another look at it. He quickly slipped out of his hammock, and gazing at its graceful lines began wishing that he had so beautiful a canoe for himself. He approached nearer and nearer, admiring it more and more, until he finally jumped in. No sooner had he done so than the vessel went off with him, and neither boat nor occupant was seen again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §156; not verbatim.

title.en: The Village of the Amazons

region.zh: 阿拉瓦克異境之旅

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §157

summary.en: They arrived at a landing-place whence an Indian house could be seen, and asked for lodging. An old woman came out and said, 'We are all females living in this settlement' — several houses, but all full of women, not a boy nor a man to be seen anywhere. 'All those who pass this way have to remain at least a year with us before we allow them to proceed on their journey. Both you, old man, and every one of your companions must take two or three of our women to wife. At the end of the year, those of you who become fathers of girls are free to go your way, but those to whom boys are born must stay with us from year to year until you beget girls.' The boat's crew made up their minds to stay — and the woman in charge was a sly old dame: to every hammock she attached a rattle, and kept awake all night; when a rattle remained silent she would proceed to that particular hammock. It was naturally many years before the crew finally got away from this settlement.
summary.zh: 至一村求宿；老嫗出曰：『此村皆女子也。』屋數椽而無一男子。『過此者必留一年乃得行。爾等各娶吾女二三；歲終生子者，女則聽去，男則留至得女乃止。』舟人無如之何，遂留。主婦甚狡：每床繫一鈴，徹夜不寐；鈴寂則親臨其床。故其去也，經年累歲矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Again they all started away, and after a time arrived at a landing-place whence an Indian house could be seen. With the old man leading his crew Indian-file up the pathway, they soon reached the house, where they asked for lodging that night. An old woman came out and said: 'We are all females living in this settlement.' This was quite true: there were several houses in the settlement, but all full of women — not a boy nor a man to be seen anywhere.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §157; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'All those who pass this way have to remain at least a year with us before we allow them to proceed on their journey. Both you, old man, and every one of your companions must take two or three of our women to wife. At the end of the year, those of you who become fathers of girls are free to go your way, but those to whom boys are born must stay with us from year to year until you beget girls. You now know what is expected of you.' The boat's crew, recognizing that there was no help for it, made up their minds to stay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §157; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now the woman in charge was indeed a sly old dame. To every hammock she attached a rattle, and then kept awake all night. If she heard the rattle sounding frequently, she knew that everything was as it should be; but when the rattle remained silent, she would proceed to that particular hammock. The men had only to give good cause for the rattles shaking all night. It was naturally many years before the crew finally got away from this settlement.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §157; not verbatim.

title.en: The Country of the Stone Adzes

region.zh: 阿拉瓦克異境之旅

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §158

summary.en: At last they arrived at the country of the stone adzes, where all the people were really stones, and some of these they brought away with them. The party finally reached home again, and the old man warned them to abstain from their wives for several nights. One of the men, however, disobeying the instructions, was punished in a very peculiar fashion by being immovably fixed.
summary.zh: 末至石鑿之國：其民皆石也；取數枚而歸。到家，老者誡以多夜毋近其妻。一人不聽，受奇罰——僵固而不得動。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: At last they arrived at the country of the stone adzes, where all the people were really stones, and some of these they brought away with them. The party finally reached home again, and the old man warned them to abstain from their wives for many nights. One of the men, however, disobeying the instructions, was punished in a very peculiar fashion by being immovably fixed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §158; not verbatim.

title.en: How Turtle Fooled the Yawarri

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞-加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §159

summary.en: It was a time of scarcity and drought, and the Bush-rat (yawarri) in his search for food came upon Turtle, also on the lookout for a bite. They discussed the hardness of the times until the question arose which of them, in case of necessity, could fast the longer. Yawarri chose a plum tree, fenced it all round, and put Turtle inside the inclosure; every month for six months he visited his captive — 'Still alive! Why not? No harm can befall me.' Then the plums ripened, the fence was broken down, and Turtle let out. Now it was Yawarri's turn: Turtle fenced him around a wild cashew tree. At the end of the third month the visits got no reply — Yawarri was no longer alive; only the flies on his dead body were alive. Yawarri did not know that the wild cashew bears fruit only once in every three or four years.
summary.zh: 歲儉而旱；刺鼠覓食遇龜，亦尋食也。因論時艱，終及孰能忍饑長久。鼠擇李樹，築籬而囚龜於內；月一問，凡六月——『尚生乎？』『生也，吾何傷。』李熟籬毀，龜乃出。次則輪鼠：龜以野腰果樹囚之。三月而問不答——鼠死矣，惟蠅生焉。鼠不知野腰果三四載方一實也。

sensitivity.note: Warrau/Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: It was a time of scarcity and drought, and the Bush-rat (yawarri) in the course of his search for food came upon Turtle, also on the lookout for a bite. After saying 'How day?' to each other and inquiring after their respective businesses, they began to discuss the hardness of the times, and thus from one thing to another, the question finally arose as to which of them in case of necessity could fast the longer. Yawarri accordingly chose a plum tree and, fencing it all round, put Turtle inside the inclosure.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §159; not verbatim.

passages.text: Every month did Yawarri visit his willing captive and ask whether he were still alive. 'Still alive! Why not? No harm can befall me,' was the reply. This was repeated once a month for six months, at the end of which time the plum-tree buds had opened, the flowers had bloomed, and the ripe fruit had fallen. So the fence was broken down and the Turtle let out. It was now Yawarri's turn to show what he could do: Turtle built him a fence around a wild cashew tree, shut him in, and went away. At the end of the third month Turtle came again, but this time he received no reply at all. Yawarri was no longer alive: only the flies on his dead body were alive. Yawarri did not know that the wild cashew bears fruit only once in every three or four years.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §159; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Turtle Tricked the Tiger

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §160

summary.en: Tiger really wanted to eat the Turtle, but was a bit of a coward, and pretended to make friends. Turtle, seeing through it, matched him at everything: strength proven with shut eyes, speed proven by a race along a path where Turtle's friends waited disguised at intervals — Tiger raced past turtle after turtle and had to admit, 'Yes, man, you have beaten me.' Then a painting contest: Tiger's slovenly handiwork is on every turtle's shell, while the beautiful spots and stripes Turtle put on him made even Tiger delighted. The stolen 'tiger-bead' necklace — 'Necklaces are of no use to the like of me; all I have is a back!' — led at last to a fight to a finish, from which Turtle slipped into a hole in a log for safety; there he still is, and there Tiger is continually on the watch for him to emerge.
summary.zh: 虎欲食龜而怯，陽與之交；龜燭其詐，事事與之敵：閉目較力，賽跑則部署親友偽龜於途——虎過龍復過龍，終曰：『誠然，汝勝我矣。』次較繪事：龜殼之紋，虎手筆也；虎身之美斑麗紋，龜筆也——虎亦自得。末因『虎珠』之失而約決死戰；龜遁入朽木之穴。今猶在焉，虎日日守之。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Tiger really wanted to eat the Turtle, but was a bit of a coward and none too sure whether his intended victim was the stronger. Wishing to find out, he approached the Turtle and pretended to make friends. The latter knew quite well what reliance could be placed on such a pretended friendship, and saw that he must exercise every craft to save himself. Tiger told him what a big strong man he was, that he ate only meat; nothing daunted, Turtle said he could do the same, suggesting their respective statements be put to the proof — during the test they should both keep their eyes shut.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §160; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Even if you are stronger than I, I am faster than you; let us have a race.' Turtle stipulated only a little time to get ready, spent the interim visiting his many friends and arranging for them to place themselves at stated intervals along the course. The two then started, and Tiger, taking a spring ahead, was soon out of sight; but Turtle slipped into the bush, took a short cut, and reached the goal, where he awaited his opponent. Tiger, racing along, met turtle after turtle — his original 'friend' had certainly arrived first — and had to admit: 'Yes, man, you have beaten me.' Then came the painting contest: just look at a turtle's shell and you will see how roughly Tiger's handiwork was done, while the beautiful spots and stripes Turtle put on him made even Tiger delighted at seeing how handsome he looked.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §160; not verbatim.

passages.text: Having gorged himself on a deer that Turtle had dropped from a dead log across its path, Tiger fell asleep, and Turtle — envious of the pretty 'tiger-bead' necklace he wore — quietly removed it and handed it to a friend. Accused, Turtle protested that necklaces were of no use to the like of him: 'I have no neck to put one on: all I have is a back!' They arranged to fight it out to a finish, going in opposite directions and returning to the same spot; but Tiger's opponent had crawled into a hole in a log for safety — and there he still is, and there Tiger is continually on the watch for him to emerge.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §160; not verbatim.

title.en: Tiger and Ant-eater

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §161

summary.en: Tiger met the Tamanoa (Great Ant-eater) in the forest and chaffed him about his funny mouth and clumsy toes. 'Even if my mouth is small and my feet are clumsy, I can eat meat quite as well as you, and I am certainly as strong as you.' They went on arguing until Tamanoa stipulated a proof — with eyes tightly closed, both should expose their droppings; while thus engaged the ant-eater surreptitiously exchanged his for his adversary's. 'Open eyes!' — Tiger examined Tamanoa's and had to admit his opponent had indeed eaten meat that very morning. 'Sick indeed you are, and weak too. Though my feet are so clumsy, I am more than a match for you.' They commenced fighting: Tiger made a spring forward at the same time that Tamanoa ducked his head; the latter, seizing Tiger by the ribs, once his hold was secure, easily crushed him — and Tiger was soon dead.
summary.zh: 虎遇大食蟻獸，嘲其口小足拙。獸曰：『口小足拙，吾亦能食肉如爾，力亦不減爾。』爭辯不已；末約閉目驗糞為證；獸乘間以己糞易之。張目！虎視獸糞，不得不認其晨曾食肉。『爾病且弱矣；吾足雖拙，足制爾。』遂鬥；虎撲而獸俯首，挾其脅，緊則碎之——虎立斃。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: One day Tiger met the Tamanoa (Great Ant-eater) in the forest, and chaffed him about his funny mouth and his clumsy toes. 'Never mind,' said Tamanoa; 'even if my mouth is small and my feet are clumsy, I can eat at all events meat quite as well as you, and I am certainly as strong as you.' 'Oh, no, indeed you are not!' replied Tiger. At last Tamanoa said he would like to have a peep into his rival's mouth, and when Tiger opened his jaws wide and showed him his fangs, told him he did not think much of them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §161; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was agreed, therefore, that the proof be made at once, Tamanoa stipulating that while thus engaged both should keep their eyes tightly closed. This also was agreed to, but while occupied in carrying out the conditions of the wager, Tamanoa surreptitiously opened his eyes and silently exchanged his droppings for those of his adversary. 'Open eyes!' shouted Ant-eater, whereupon both turned around. When Tiger went to examine Tamanoa's, he had to admit at once that his opponent had indeed eaten meat, and a goodly quantity of it, that very morning. 'Sick indeed you are, and weak too,' retorted Tamanoa; 'for though my feet are so clumsy from walking always on their outsides, I am more than a match for you.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §161; not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger was much angered at this last remark, and the result was that they commenced fighting. Tiger made a spring forward at the same time that Tamanoa ducked his head; the latter, seizing Tiger by the ribs, once his hold was secure, easily crushed him — and Tiger was soon dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §161; not verbatim.

title.en: The Water Serpent's Skin: How Birds Got Their Plumage

region.zh: 圭亞那（據布雷特）

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §162

summary.en: Once upon a time there was a Water Serpent, a huge creature with a most brilliant skin of red, yellow, green, black, and white in extraordinary patterns. He became such a terror to all other living creatures that the men and birds — who were friends in those days — combined forces to destroy him, the creature's skin being promised to the first one who made him come out of the pool. All were afraid to tackle him except Cormorant, who darted down into the water, drove an arrow through his neck — fastened by a string to a tree on the bank — and finally drew him to land, where he was skinned. Cormorant claimed the skin, and the warriors told him he could have it; he nodded to the other birds, who, each seizing part of the edge, bore it to a secluded spot, where each took the part he had helped to carry. Each bird carried his load home on his back, and ever since has been marked by the hues of the section of the serpent's skin — parrots green, macaws scarlet and gold, and so on. But Cormorant as his share got only the snake's head with its somber tints; however, he remained content with this.
summary.zh: 昔有水蛇，其皮紅黃綠黑白，斑斕奪目；為萬物之患。人與鳥——古相友也——合力誅之；約曰：先誘之出水者得皮。惟鸕鶿敢下，箭貫其頸，繫繩於樹，曳之登陸而剝之。群鳥各持其邊，運至僻處，各取所負之段歸——故鸚鵡綠、金剛猩紅而金，各從其皮。鸕鶿所得惟蛇首，色暗；然彼自足焉。

sensitivity.note: Guiana tradition from Brett 1880, retold in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

Each bird carried his load home on his back, and ever since has been marked by the hues of the section of the serpent's skin that he happened to bear — parrots green, macaws scarlet and gold, and so on. title.en: How the Tapir Punished the Indian

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §163B

summary.en: Traveling through the forest one day an Indian came across a party of men seated, eating something that smelt very savory. Instead of waiting to be asked, he roughly inquired what they were smacking their lips over. They told him it was bush-cow (tapir) liver, and that if he wanted some he would have to hunt it himself; on further questioning they told him exactly where he would find one sleeping, and advised him that the best and quickest way to get the liver was to insert the knife from behind — and the silly old fool believed them. He found the beast asleep, inserted his arm — and with the tapir now wide awake he found it impossible to release it. On rushed the animal through thicket, bush, and forest, dragging the miserable hunter behind him, night and day, only to be released when they found themselves on a sheet of water. By the time the man reached home all the skin had peeled off his arm, and when his folk asked what had caused the trouble, they laughed at him: he had been punished for his want of manners.
summary.zh: 一印第安人遇眾食香物；不待請而粗問之。眾曰：貘肝也；欲食則自獵。又告以貘睡之所，且教以『從後取肝最捷』——愚者信之。至則臂入而獸醒，不可拔；貘奔林越莽，晝夜曳之，至水濱方釋。歸時臂皮盡脫；家人聞而大笑——無禮之罰也。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: While traveling through the forest one day an Indian came across a party of men seated, eating something that smelt very savory. Now, instead of waiting to be asked to partake of the cheer, our traveler roughly inquired of them what it was that they were smacking their lips over. They told him that it was bush-cow [tapir] liver, and that if he wanted some he would have to hunt it himself. On further questioning, they told him exactly where he would find a bush-cow sleeping, and advised him of the best and quickest way to get the liver — and the silly old fool believed them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163B; not verbatim.

On rushed the animal through thicket, bush, and forest, dragging the miserable hunter behind him. By the time the man reached home all the skin had peeled off his arm, and when his folk asked him what had caused the trouble, he told them — and they laughed at him. title.en: Sisters Bush-cow and Water-cow

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. IX 'Animals as Sentient Human Beings', §163D

summary.en: There was once a lovely big plum tree, and two sisters would come regularly and pick the fruit. A bush-cow (tapir) came along one day; they squeezed some of the fruit into a manicole-palm spathe and offered it to him to drink — until in a very short time he became so tame that all the girls had to do was whistle, and he appeared immediately. Their brothers became suspicious, set a watch, and killed the beast, bringing the meat home, which all shared. The girls whistled the customary whistle — but no Bush-cow came. 'That is our pet whom you have killed,' they said, left the house crying, and at the river bank the younger sister slipped into the water: 'People will henceforth call me water-cow' — diving three times, she came up finally entirely in the shape of that creature. The elder sister rushed into the bush and changed herself into a Bush-cow. Bush-cow and water-cow often meet nowadays at the waterside and have a chat: haven't they both the same talk?
summary.zh: 有大李樹，二姊妹日往採果。一貘至；以棕苞承果漿飼之；未幾馴，哨聲一呼即至。二兄疑而窺之，遂殺之，攜肉歸，共食。姊妹仍往，吹哨而貘不至。曰：『此吾儕所愛而爾所殺也。』泣而出，至河；妹入水曰：『今後人呼我為水牛。』三沒而出，化為海牛。姊入林化為貘。今二者恆會於水濱相語——其鳴一也，安得不解？

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was once a lovely big plum tree, and two sisters would come regularly and pick the fruit. One day while thus busily engaged a Bush-cow [tapir] came along, so they squeezed some of the fruit into a manicole-palm spathe and offered it to him to drink. He drank it. Next day the same thing happened, and so on day by day, until in a very short time he became so tame that all the girls had to do when they reached the tree was just to give a little whistle, when he would put in an appearance immediately.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163D; not verbatim.

passages.text: Their two brothers, however, became suspicious of the young women's frequent absences from home, and setting a watch, saw them whistle for and then feed the creature with squeezed plums. 'What does this mean? Why tame a wild-cow?' Realizing something to be wrong, they made up their minds to kill the beast: leaving their sisters in the house one morning, they made straight for the tree, squeezed some of the fruit, and, imitating their sisters' whistle, called the Tapir — and shot him as soon as he came near, cut up the meat, and brought it home, where all had their share in eating it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163D; not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the girls repaired as usual to the plum tree, squeezed some of the fruit into a spathe, and gave the customary whistle — but no Bush-cow came. They went home and began to cry, refusing to be comforted. 'That is our pet whom you have killed,' they said, and left the house crying all the way to a river bank, where the younger sister attempted to jump into the water. She managed to slip in, and coming to the surface exclaimed: 'People will henceforth call me water-cow.' Then, diving three times, she came up finally entirely in the shape of that creature. The elder sister thereupon rushed into the bush, and changed herself into a Bush-cow. Bush-cow and water-cow often meet nowadays at the waterside and have a chat — haven't they both the same talk?
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163D; not verbatim.

title.en: The First Makuari Whips

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. X 'Spirits of the Bush: Associated with Particular Plants', §163A

summary.en: There was a family of two sisters and two brothers. Cutting firewood, the sisters split a log and found inside a pretty little whip; each made another exactly like it, hung the three whips in a little banab in their field, and took their own jug of drink there on three occasions. The brothers, suspecting, sent the little hummingbird to make inquiries, then asked the sisters to explain — and to let them look on while the girls sported with the whips. At the banab the women showed their manner of play, but it was soon evident they knew neither how to sing, to dance, nor to whip properly; constrained after repeated entreaties, they handed the whips over to their brothers, who showed them how the real thing ought to be done — and 'called' their sisters Kumaka-plait and Ite-fiber, the elder and younger, transforming them into the kumaka thread and ite fiber out of which the Arawaks have ever since made their makuari whips.
summary.zh: 家有二妹二兄。姊妹伐薪剖木，得一美鞭於木中；各仿製一鞭，懸三鞭於田中小棚，三度自攜酒往。兄疑，遣蜂鳥偵之，遂詰其妹；妹不許兄執鞭，惟許其觀。妹之歌舞與鞭皆不精；至再四懇求，乃以鞭付兄，兄示其真法——且『呼』其妹為庫瑪卡編與伊特縴，化之為庫瑪卡縶與伊特縴——阿拉瓦克人至今制瑪庫阿利鞭，用此二材也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was a family of two sisters and two brothers. Going out one day to cut firewood, the sisters proceeded to the forest and cut the timber; on splitting a log, they found inside a pretty little whip. After closely examining it, each girl proceeded to make another exactly like it. Then they proceeded to their provision field, put up a little banab, and hung inside it the three whips; when they reached home they made some drink, two jugsful altogether, one for their two brothers and one for themselves — they took their portion to the banab, where they left it, and did this on three occasions.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163A; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers, suspecting that something was wrong, sent the little hummingbird to make inquiries: the bird flew into the banab, saw the jug of drink there and the three whips hanging up, and reported accordingly. The sisters, admitting the whips, refused to deliver their charge over to anyone — but they let the brothers come and look at them sporting with them. The women did their play, but it was soon evident that they knew neither how to sing, to dance, nor to whip properly with them; after repeated entreaties they finally handed the whips over to their brothers, who now showed them how the real thing ought to be done.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163A; not verbatim.

passages.text: Furthermore, they 'called' their sisters Kussaro-banna and Koro-botio — the elder and the younger — that is, they transformed them into kumaka [Bromelia] thread and ite fiber, the two materials out of which the Arawaks have ever since made their makuari whips.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §163A; not verbatim.

title.en: Milómaki and the Paxiuba Flutes of the Sun's House
title.zh: 米洛馬基與日宮之帕希巴笛

region.zh: 哥倫比亞亞馬遜阿帕波里斯河亞烏納之地

texts.period: Yahuna oral tradition recorded by Koch-Grünberg; retold 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. X 'Spirits of the Bush', §163A (from Koch-Grünberg)

summary.en: A long time ago, from out of the great Water-house — the house of the Sun — came a little boy, Milómaki, who sang so beautifully that everyone came from far and near to hear him; but when they reached their settlements again, all died. Their relatives came and burned him on a large pyre, but he continued singing until he died; thus his body was destroyed, but his spirit went up to heaven. From the ashes grew a long green leaf, which visibly became greater and greater and turned into the first Paxiuba palm — the timber used for all kinds of weapons and articles. The people made big flutes of this tree, which produced the same melodies Milómaki had sung. To honor him the men dance and blow on these flutes nowadays when the various fruits are ripe, because it was he who created them all; the women and children must not see these flutes: the former would die, and the latter would eat earth, become sick, and die.
summary.zh: 上古自大水屋——日之宮——出一小兒，名米洛馬基；歌聲之美，遠近來聽；然眾歸村皆死。親屬焚之於巨薪；火中歌聲不絕而卒。其體雖燬，靈升天。灰中生長綠葉，日大，化為第一株帕希巴棕——製武器百物之材也。眾以之製大笛，聲如米洛馬基之歌。果熟之期，男子吹笛舞之以祀之——蓋百果皆彼所造。婦孺毋得見此笛：婦見則死，兒見則食土、病、死。

title.en: The Spirit of the Rot Saves the Young Woman

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. X 'Spirits of the Bush', §167A

summary.en: Two girls were left in charge while the household went to a drink-party. About sunset a Yurokon emerged from a neighboring silk-cotton tree, shot a parrot, and asked them to cook it. After they had eaten and he had slung his hammock, he called on the younger sister, who sent the elder instead; later she heard extraordinary growlings, found her sister lying dead with blood trickling to the ground, and hid herself in a stack of buck-corn all mildewed and rotten, warning the Spirit of the Rot that if the Yurokon caught her she would never supply him with any more corn. By dawn the Yurokon could not find her and had to hurry back to his home in the silk-cotton tree. The parents made a ring of fire round the komaka tree and threw twenty basketsful of peppers into the flames: down came small baboons, then bigger ones, and at last the very Yurokon — clubbed to death, 'in payment for my daughter', with woman's flesh found in his belly. The younger sister obeyed her parents from that time onward.
summary.zh: 家人赴宴，留二女守屋。日暮，林鬼自棉樹出，射鸚鵡令烹；食罷召季女，季遣長姊往。夜聞異吼，火照見姊屍血流於地；季匿於黴腐之玉蜀黍堆，且告黴神：『若縱鬼獲我，永不供粟。』黎明鬼索之不得，歸棉樹。父母環樹舉火，投椒二十筐；小狒狒、大狒狒相繼墜而斃；末鬼亦墜，擊殺之——『以償我女』——剖其腹，得人肉。季女自此孝順。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Two girls were left in charge while the remainder of the household went to a drink-party. About sunset a Yurokon emerged from a neighboring silk-cotton tree: he had an arrow and with it he shot a parrot. He brought the bird to the young women and asked them to cook it, and they, not knowing that he was a Bush Spirit, were only too ready to oblige him. After they had eaten the bird and he had slung his hammock, Yurokon called on the younger sister to join him, but she, not feeling so inclined, sent her sister instead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §167A; not verbatim.

passages.text: Later, when all was still and dark, the younger sister heard extraordinary noises and growling proceeding from their visitor's hammock; blowing up the fire, she went over to Yurokon's hammock, whence she saw blood trickling to the ground — inside, her sister lay dead. She now recognized the tribe to which the man belonged, and hastened to save herself: she had a stack of buck-corn which had all become mildewed and rotten, and in this corn she hid herself, warning the Spirit of the Rot that if he allowed the Yurokon to come and catch her, she would never supply him with any more corn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §167A; not verbatim.

passages.text: By very early dawn Yurokon had completed his work of destruction with the elder sister, and now asked the Spirit of the Rot whether he had not seen another woman about; but this Spirit refused to answer, being so busily engaged in eating the corn. At daybreak he had to hurry back to his home in the silk-cotton tree. The parents picked all the peppers around — twenty basketsful — made a ring of fire right round the komaka [silk-cotton] tree, and threw peppers into the flames: down came a lot of small baboons, of which the fire made short shrift; then bigger baboons; and at last the very Yurokon who had killed their elder daughter, clubbed to death — 'I am killing you in payment for my daughter' — with woman's flesh found in his belly. The younger sister obeyed her parents from that time onward.

title.en: The Ite Palm and the Mora Tree

region.zh: 莫魯卡至奧里諾科瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. X 'Spirits of the Bush', §168C

summary.en: In the days of long ago there was always to be found growing a Mora near an Ite: wherever one was to be seen, there close by would be found the other. The Baboon would forage on the Ite and eat of her fruit, and this made the Mora jealous — for these two trees must have been women, did they not each bear seed? The Ite said she would leave the Mora and travel eastward, but the Mora followed her, wanting the Baboon to come and stay with her. On and on they traveled east, leaving seeds behind, the ground changing from dry bush to swamp; the Baboon more and more preferred to feed on the Mora, whose branches were always well above the water, and finally left the Ite altogether. The Mora remained satisfied where she was, while the Ite traveled still farther eastward, stopping only at the heavy swamps of the Orinoco — where there was too much water for the Baboon to follow her. Hence the Baboon is never met with nowadays on the Ite palms but always on the topmost branches of the Mora; and all the Ite palms more or less isolated in this district are stragglers from the original palm which traveled to the Orinoco, where the real Ite palms yield starch and fruit and drink in plenty.
summary.zh: 上古摩拉必傍伊特而生。狒狒食伊特之果，摩拉妒之——二樹蓋皆女也，非各結實乎？伊特欲東行，摩拉隨之，欲致狒狒於己。東行日遠，沿途遺種；地由燥林而為沼，狒狒漸就摩拉，以其枝高出水面也，遂棄伊特。摩拉止於其所；伊特行至奧里諾科大沼乃止——水太深，狒狒不能從。故今狒狒不見於伊特，而恆在摩拉之巔；此間零落之伊特，皆行者之遺也；真伊特在奧里諾科，粉與果與酒皆豐。

passages.text: In the days of long ago there was always to be found growing a Mora near an Ite: wherever one was to be seen, there sure enough, close by, would be found the other. The Baboon would forage on the Ite and eat of her fruit, and this is just what made the Mora jealous. In those times the trees, like the animals, would converse with one another just as people do; and these two trees must have been women, for did they not each bear seed?

passages.text: At any rate the Ite said she would leave the Mora and travel eastward, but the Mora followed her: she wanted the Baboon to come and stay with her, and was very jealous. As they both traveled on and on toward the east, they left some of their seeds behind; the ground gradually changed from dry bush to swamp, the Baboon more and more preferred to feed on the Mora, whose branches were always well above the water surface, and so finally left the Ite altogether.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §168C; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Mora now at last satisfied, and with no further cause for jealousy, remained where she was, while the Ite traveled still farther eastward, stopping only when she came to the heavy swamps of the Orinoco — where there was too much water for the Baboon to follow her. Hence it happens that the Baboon is never met with nowadays on the Ite palms, but always on the topmost branches of the Mora. All the Ite palms that you see here and there more or less isolated in this district are stragglers from the original palm which traveled to the Orinoco; it is only on that mighty stream where you see the real Ite palms, which yield starch and fruit and drink in plenty.
